summaries.example: Imagine a game about a sentence: “The king is sitting or you are in Rome.” At first, you do not know whether the king is sitting, so you say you are unsure. Then you learn that you are not in Rome. Now the first sentence must be true, because one of its two parts has been ruled out. Heytesbury used games like this to show how new information can change what a careful thinker should say.
summaries.summary: William Heytesbury was a fourteenth-century scholar connected with Oxford’s Merton College and the group called the Oxford Calculators. He wrote about difficult logic puzzles, knowledge, the meanings of words, and arguments. He also studied motion and change. One important idea, the Middle Degree Theorem, says that an object whose speed increases evenly travels the same distance as an object moving at its middle speed for the same amount of time. Heytesbury often used imagined cases and question-and-answer games to test ideas. His work helped connect careful reasoning with mathematical studies of nature, and later scholars in Britain and Italy continued to discuss it.
key_ideas: Heytesbury studied logic, mathematics, and nature together.
In his logic games, answers could change when new information was added.
He carefully studied what words stand for in sentences.
He described changing motion with mathematical rules, including a rule about average speed.
His writings influenced later thinkers in Britain, Italy, and elsewhere.
summaries.why_it_matters: Heytesbury shows that philosophy can be like solving a puzzle. We need to notice what a sentence means, what we know, and what follows from earlier information. His work also shows how people studied motion mathematically before modern physics had taken its later form. Learning about him helps us see that ideas can develop over many centuries.

important_terms.definition: A person’s reasoning about what is true, false, or uncertain.
A practice game in which one player gives assumptions and another answers while trying not to contradict anything.
A tricky sentence or argument that looks correct but needs careful checking.
A rule about motion: when speed rises evenly, the distance traveled matches traveling at the middle speed for the same time.

questions_to_think_about: Why might an answer change when new information is added?
Is a sentence about knowing something always the same as knowing that the sentence is true?
How could average speed help us understand a moving object?

summaries.example: Suppose an argument says: “If the lamp is on, the room is bright; the room is bright; therefore the lamp is on.” This conclusion does not follow in every situation, because sunlight or another lamp could make the room bright. Heytesbury’s approach asks whether a counterexample is possible. If one is, the inference is not valid in the strongest, universal sense. It might still work in a restricted setting where the lamp is the only possible source of light.
summaries.summary: William Heytesbury, a member of the Oxford Calculators, developed a broad program linking medieval logic, semantics, epistemic analysis, and mathematical natural philosophy. In obligationes, an opponent establishes a casus and proposes sentences; the respondent must concede, deny, or doubt them while preserving consistency. Because relevance is assessed against the whole history of the game, a sentence’s proper response can change. Heytesbury also analyzes supposition, ampliation, and the distinction between mentioning an expression and using it. His account of validity includes truth-preservation tested against possible or imaginable countercases, while distinguishing universal formal validity from validity restricted by subject matter. In epistemic logic, he uses the Aristotelian de re/de dicto distinction and treats knowledge as requiring truth, while resisting unrestricted closure of knowledge under every implication. In natural philosophy, he studies limits and continuously varying quantities. His Middle Degree Theorem states that uniformly accelerated or decelerated motion covers the distance associated with the middle speed over the same time. He also examines self-referential paradoxes, offering a consistency-based treatment while acknowledging that objections remain.
key_ideas: Heytesbury’s obligationes treat reasoning as a dynamic consistency-maintenance game. A sentence may become relevant after later moves.
He distinguishes what is possible from what is merely imaginable for the purposes of a logical dispute.
His theory of supposition analyzes whether a term is being mentioned or used and how its reference works in context.
He describes deductive validity at several levels: universal formal validity, restricted validity based on content, and ordinary truth-preservation.
His analysis of knowledge separates de re and de dicto readings and accepts some principles about knowledge while rejecting stronger forms of logical omniscience.
His speculative physics uses limits, ratios, and degrees to analyze beginnings, capacities, local motion, alteration, and increase in size.
summaries.why_it_matters: Heytesbury illustrates how medieval philosophy did not sharply separate logic, language, knowledge, mathematics, and physics. His methods show the importance of testing an inference by its form, its content, and possible counterexamples. His treatment of changing motion also belongs to a longer history of mathematical physics: the Middle Degree Theorem was discussed by later scholars and eventually became relevant to the history of accounts of free fall. His work therefore matters both for the history of logic and for the development of scientific reasoning.

important_terms.definition: A fourteenth-century Oxford movement that joined logical analysis with mathematical approaches to natural philosophy.
A formal consistency game: an opponent proposes assumptions and sentences, while a respondent answers without contradiction.
A difficult argument or sentence used to test logical, semantic, or physical rules.
The relation between a term and what it stands for in a particular sentence.
A method of testing an inference by asking whether its premises could be true while its conclusion is false.
The distinction between knowing that an identified object has a property and knowing that a description as a whole is true.
A sentence that refers to itself in a way that produces a truth-related contradiction, such as a statement saying it is false.
Heytesbury’s rule that uniform change in speed can be measured by the corresponding middle speed over the same interval.

questions_to_think_about: Should a logically valid inference work in every possible subject matter, or can validity depend on a restricted domain?
What is the difference between knowing that a person is running and knowing that a particular named person is running?
Can an impossible situation still be useful in a thought experiment?
Why might a theory of knowledge accept positive introspection but not negative introspection?
How does the Middle Degree Theorem connect a changing speed with an equivalent constant speed?

summaries.example: A teacher writes, “All birds can fly,” and asks whether it is true. You might think of a penguin and disagree. But imagine that the class is discussing only ordinary birds found near the school. In that special discussion, the sentence might be accepted for a limited purpose, though it would not be correct everywhere. Heytesbury’s studies of arguments asked similar questions: Does an argument work in every situation, or only when extra facts are assumed?
summaries.summary: William Heytesbury was a fourteenth-century scholar at Oxford and part of the Oxford Calculators, a group interested in logic, mathematics, and natural philosophy. Much of his writing examines sophisms, which are difficult cases that expose hidden problems in reasoning. In obligationes, an opponent sets up a situation and makes claims, while a respondent must say whether each claim is accepted, rejected, or uncertain. Heytesbury’s distinctive approach evaluates claims in light of the entire sequence of the debate, so a claim that was initially unrelated can later follow from new information. He also investigates how terms refer to things, how meanings can be extended to possible or future objects, and how arguments should be tested. In epistemic logic, he distinguishes two readings of statements about knowing: one about an object with a property and another about knowing a complete proposition. In natural philosophy, he studies change through limits and ratios. His Middle Degree Theorem connects uniformly changing speed with the distance covered at an intermediate speed. His work was later read and debated in Britain, Italy, and Central Europe.
key_ideas: Heytesbury used debate-like logic games to study consistency and relevance.
A sentence can be relevant because it follows from earlier moves, or irrelevant because it does not.
He distinguished possible situations from impossible situations that can still be imagined without an obvious contradiction.
He studied how terms work in context, including how their reference can be widened to past, future, or merely possible things.
He described different kinds of validity, including validity in every subject matter and validity only in a limited setting.
His account of motion used mathematical ideas about speed, limits, and changing qualities.
summaries.why_it_matters: Heytesbury’s work matters because it treats reasoning as something that must be checked step by step. It asks us to distinguish what a sentence says, what a speaker knows, and what truly follows from earlier claims. His mathematical treatment of motion also shows that important ideas in physics can have a long history, with medieval analyses contributing to later discussions even though they used a different philosophical framework.

important_terms.definition: A late-medieval group at Oxford known for combining logic, mathematics, and the study of nature.
A structured debate in which one person gives assumptions and another must answer while avoiding contradiction.
A puzzling argument or sentence designed to test whether a rule really works.
The way a word or phrase stands for something within a particular sentence.
A possible case showing that an argument’s conclusion does not follow from its starting points.
A difference between knowing a fact about a thing and knowing that a full description of the thing is true.
A self-referential puzzle that creates a problem about truth and falsity.
A rule saying that evenly increasing speed can be replaced, for distance traveled, by the middle speed over the same time.

questions_to_think_about: What makes a counterexample powerful against an argument?
Can an impossible idea still help someone reason carefully?
Why might the meaning of a word depend on the sentence in which it appears?
What is gained by separating “I know a person is running” from “I know that Socrates is running”?
Why would a philosopher study motion through imagined cases?
